“Do you have them?”

“Yes.”

“Did he seem upset?”

“No.”

“Poor man!”

That “Poor man!” was uttered in a tone impossible to convey. Marguerite took the six thousand-franc notes.

“It was time,” she said. “My dear Prudence, do you need any money?”

“You know, my child, that the fifteenth is in two days; if you could lend me three or four hundred francs, you would be doing me a favor.”

“Send someone tomorrow morning; it is too late to get them changed.”

“Do not forget.”

“Do not worry. Are you having supper with us?”

“No, Charles is waiting for me at home.”

“So you are still mad about him?”

“Besotted, my dear! Until tomorrow. Goodbye, Armand.”

Madame Duvernoy went out.

Marguerite opened her cabinet and tossed the banknotes inside.

“You will permit me to go to bed!” she said, smiling and moving toward her bed.

“Not only do I permit you, I beg you to.”

She threw the guipure coverlet back over the foot of her bed and lay down.

“Now,” she said, “come and sit beside me, and let us talk.”

Prudence was right: the answer she had brought Marguerite had cheered her.

“Do you forgive me for my bad temper this evening?” she said to me, taking my hand.

“I am ready to forgive you many other things besides.”

“And do you love me?”

“To the point of madness.”

“In spite of my bad temper?”

“In spite of everything.”

“You swear it to me!”

“Yes,” I said to her softly.

Nanine then came in carrying plates, a cold chicken, a bottle of Bordeaux, strawberries, and two place settings.

“I did not have any punch made for you,” Nanine said. “Bordeaux is better for you. Is that not so, monsieur?”

“Certainly,” I replied, still deeply moved by Marguerite’s last words and gazing ardently at her.

“Good,” she said. “Put all that on the little table and bring it close to the bed; we shall serve ourselves. You have been up for three nights; you must want to sleep. Go to bed; I need nothing more.”

“Should I double-lock the door?”

“I should think so! And above all, say that no one is to be let in tomorrow before noon.”




Chapter XII


At five in the morning, when daylight began to show through the curtains, Marguerite said to me:

“Forgive me for sending you away, but I must. The duke comes every morning; when he comes, he will be told that I am asleep, and he may wait for me to wake up.”

I took Marguerite’s head in my hands, her loosened hair streaming around her, and gave her one last kiss, saying:

“When shall I see you again?”

“Listen,” she went on, “take that little gold key on the mantelpiece, go and open that door, bring the key back here, and leave. During the day, you will receive a letter and my instructions, for you know that you must obey blindly.”

“Yes, and what if I were to ask for something already?”

“What?”

“That you let me keep this key.”

“I have never done for anyone what you are asking of me.”

“Well, do it for me, for I swear to you that I do not love you as the others loved you.”

“Very well, keep it; but I warn you that it rests solely with me to make that key of no use to you.”

“Why?”

“There are bolts on the inside of the door.”

“Wicked woman!”

“I shall have them removed.”

“So you love me a little?”

“I do not know how it has happened, but it seems to me that I do. Now go; I am falling asleep.”

We remained in each other’s arms for a few seconds, and I left.

The streets were deserted; the great city was still asleep; a gentle coolness ran through those districts that the noise of men would invade a few hours later.

It seemed to me that this sleeping city belonged to me; I searched my memory for the names of those whose happiness I had envied until then, and I could not recall a single one without finding myself happier than he.

To be loved by a chaste young girl, to be the first to reveal to her that strange mystery of love, is certainly a great joy, but it is the simplest thing in the world. To take possession of a heart unaccustomed to attack is to enter an open and ungarrisoned city. Education, a sense of duty, and family are very strong sentinels; but no sentinels are so vigilant that they cannot be deceived by a sixteen-year-old girl to whom nature, through the voice of the man she loves, gives its first counsels of love, all the more ardent because they seem all the purer.

The more the young girl believes in goodness, the more readily she surrenders herself, if not to the lover, at least to love; for, being without mistrust, she is without strength, and to make oneself loved by her is a triumph that any man of twenty-five may grant himself whenever he wishes. And this is so true that you need only see how young girls are surrounded with watchfulness and ramparts! Convents do not have walls high enough, mothers locks strong enough, religion duties constant enough to keep all those charming birds shut in their cages, upon which no one even takes the trouble to scatter flowers. How they must long for that world hidden from them, how enticing they must believe it to be, how they must listen to the first voice that comes through the bars to tell them its secrets, and bless the hand that first lifts a corner of the mysterious veil.

But to be truly loved by a courtesan is a far more difficult victory. In them, the body has worn out the soul, the senses have burned up the heart, and debauchery has armored the feelings. The words spoken to them, they have long known; the methods employed, they know; the very love they inspire, they have sold. They love as a profession and not from impulse. They are better guarded by their calculations than a virgin by her mother and her convent; and so they have invented the word caprice for those loves without commerce that they allow themselves from time to time as a respite, an excuse, or a consolation; like those usurers who extort money from a thousand people and believe they redeem everything by one day lending twenty francs to some poor devil dying of hunger, without demanding interest or asking him for a receipt.”
